title: Learned sensor labels reveal different hen behavior transitions across housing
summary: A learned inertial-sensor classifier was used to compare behavior in cages and floor pens in five laying hens. Floor pens showed more detected transitions involving several comfort and activity behaviors. The small repeated-measure experiment does not establish a general welfare scale, and housing-specific classifier errors may affect comparisons.
ai_technology: Multilayer perceptron behavior classification from accelerometer and gyroscope features
organization: Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology

evidence.tested: A two-hen labeled training/evaluation step supplied separate housing-specific classifiers. A later recording step used five hens in both housing systems, averaging 4.5 recording days per bird/housing condition. Those later recordings were not reused training data. The source reports more detected transitions involving moving, preening, dust-bathing, litter scratching, resting, tail-wagging and body shaking in floor pens. Visual-scan comparison in a sampled floor-pen video gave correlation .94.
evidence.unknown: There were only five birds in the housing comparison; repeated days/intervals are not independent birds. Basic same-bird classification accuracy differed substantially by housing (77.5% cages, 96.3% floor pens), and overlapping sensor windows may affect internal validation. The source does not establish that differential errors cannot explain part of the transition contrast. Training-bird overlap with the later five-bird population is not excluded, although recording data were separate. Pooling days and thresholding transitions do not establish a population-general causal welfare measure. Spatial location came from a colored marker rather than a learned tracking model.
evidence.ai_role: The trained multilayer classifier converted sensor streams into behavior labels; conventional temporal counting/statistical comparisons then quantified the source-specific housing contrast.

source_review.scope: Original computational training/partition Methods, represented applied Results and relevant limitations actually read; no source code executed.
